The sigmoid (or logistic) function maps any real number z into the open interval (0, 1). As z grows large and positive, e⁻ᶻ shrinks toward 0, so σ(z) approaches 1. As z becomes very negative, e⁻ᶻ explodes, pulling σ(z) toward 0. At z = 0, the function passes through exactly 0.5 — the natural decision midpoint.

Because σ(z) ≥ 0.5 exactly when z ≥ 0, this threshold on the probability translates back into a condition on the raw linear score: predict class 1 whenever θᵀx ≥ 0. Geometrically, the equation θᵀx = 0 defines a hyperplane in feature space — a straight line in 2D, a flat plane in 3D. Everything on one side is classified as 1, everything on the other side as 0.
A linear score θᵀx is squashed by the sigmoid into a valid probability P(y=1|x).
